title: CloudWatch & X-Ray Observability
summary: Metrics, alarms, logs and traces that drive scaling, failover and troubleshooting.
tldr: **CloudWatch metrics + alarms** drive automation: Auto Scaling, Route 53 health checks, ECS rollbacks, SNS notifications and EC2 actions.
Memory, disk usage and app logs from inside an instance need the **CloudWatch agent**; the hypervisor can't see them.
**X-Ray** traces one request end to end across API Gateway, Lambda, and downstream calls, and draws a **service map** to find the slow component.
Pick metrics that match the business objective: ALB 5XX for errors, `HealthyHostCount` for capacity, SQS `ApproximateAgeOfOldestMessage` for processing delay.

keyFacts.text: EC2 sends basic metrics every 5 minutes. **Detailed monitoring** sends them every minute for faster scaling and alarms.
**High-resolution custom metrics** can be published at 1-second granularity for alarms that react within seconds.
A **composite alarm** combines other alarms with AND/OR logic, which reduces alarm noise and false pages.
Scale SQS workers on a custom **backlog-per-instance** metric (queue depth ÷ running instances), not on CPU.
**CloudWatch Logs Insights** runs ad hoc queries over log groups; metric filters turn log patterns into metrics you can alarm on.

traps: CloudTrail records API calls, not request latency. It can't show where a request spent its time.
VPC Flow Logs show IP traffic metadata, not application-level timing.
An average metric hides intermittent slow requests. Traces or percentiles (p99) reveal them.
EC2 status checks don't see an app that hangs. Use ELB health checks or app-level metrics.
To investigate a live instance without it being replaced or receiving traffic, put it in Auto Scaling **Standby**, rather than detaching it or suspending processes.
